transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-07-28
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Tom Rivera (VP Ops, Lattice Systems), Maya Liu (SRE Lead), Evan Park (Security)

Auto-summary (auto): Lattice Systems is evaluating Redwood Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private. Primary concerns: predictable SLA during regional outages, graceful degradation strategies, certification/KMS needs, and cost tradeoffs for reserved capacity. They want a benchmark and an SLA mapping doc.

Topics: SLA targets, multi-region routing, canary + fallback policies, cache warming, KMS/HSM, SOC2/ISO attestation, pilot scope.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Alex (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, Tom, Maya, Evan, thanks for making time. Quick intro, I'm Alex Chen, AE on the Redwood infra team; Priya is our SE who will go through some technical bits.
[00:40] Tom (VP Ops): Yeah thanks, Alex. We're trying to nail down operational guardrails for our LLM endpoints, mostly around what happens when a region degrades or a GPU pool is saturated. We use the term "graceful degradation" internally.
[01:20] Priya (SE): Totally. We'll walk through routing options, fallback chains, and how Dedicated or Private changes the game. Quick Q to start — do you expect sustained p95 latencies under like 200ms for the user-facing path?
[02:00] Maya (SRE): For interactive flows yeah we want < 250ms p95 ideally. But we can accept higher if the model quality reduces gracefully. The real problem is unpredictable tail when incidents and cross-region failover occurs.
[02:40] Evan (Security): Also, from a security side we need to know where keys live, KMS vs HSM, and if audit logs capture per-request metadata. We can't have tokens stored in plain S3 without encryption.
[03:20] Alex (AE): Absolutely. Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS and we have HSM integrations on the roadmap — but we'll share the SOC2/ISO attestations and our KMS pattern in the deck.
[04:00] Priya (SE): On the routing side, Redwood supports policy-based routing: latency-first, cost-first, or tiered routing by customer tier. For Dedicated you can reserve capacity in multiple regions and use active-active or active-passive.
[04:40] Tom (VP Ops): Active-active sounds good in theory but last time we tried geo-split we saw session affinity issues — the model KV cache didn't warm. How do you handle KV cache warming across regions?
[05:20] Priya (SE): Good call. We do prefix/KV cache warming and have an optional sticky routing mode for session affinity. When you fail over, we can either rebuild KV cache on cold start (slower) or route to a warm standby model variant with truncated cache. There's a tradeoff between startup latency and output consistency.
[06:00] Maya (SRE): If we route to a smaller quantized model as fallback, what's the typical quality delta? Our acceptance tests will need to flag hallucination regressions.
[06:40] Priya (SE): It depends on model family and quantization. Redwood's Optimize suggests quant profiles that tend to keep NLL drops minimal for conversational tasks; we also support automated evals tied to your prompt set so regressions are caught.
[07:20] Tom: From SLA perspective are you willing to map availability tiers to fallback behaviors? e.g., 99.95% we fail to another region with same model; below 99.9% maybe we degrade to a smaller model but keep latency?
[08:00] Alex: We can propose an SLA mapping doc. Common pattern — hard SLA for availability to hosted API with 99.9/99.95 for Dedicated. For Private, SLA is more about the control plane availability and support terms. We'll draft options aligned with your RTO/RPO.
[08:40] Evan: Also curious about error budgets and incident escalation. What metrics do you expose for customer alerting?
[09:20] Priya: Token-level latency, per-route error rate, model fallback counts, queue length, and per-request trace IDs. You can set alert thresholds and we provide tracing hooks so you can plug into your pager.
[10:00] Tom: Good. For multi-region, do you manage DNS-level steering or use anycast/TCP? We prefer application-layer steering to keep sticky sessions consistent.
[10:40] Priya: We do policy-based steering at the edge and per-route session sticky options. We don't recommend DNS-only steering for session-affinity workloads because DNS TTLs complicate quick failover.
[11:20] Maya: For autoscaling, during big spikes, how do you prevent noisy neighbor from choking our high-priority routes on Dedicated?
[12:00] Alex: Dedicated lets you carve out GPU pools and apply QoS by route; you can reserve headroom, set burst capacity policies, and we support route-weighting to prioritize traffic. We'll show the capacity worksheet.
[12:40] Evan: Any limits on model variants for fallback? We have a lineage policy, can't run un-vetted models in prod.
[13:20] Priya: You can pin model versions and Redwood supports canary rollouts and automatic fallback to pre-approved variants only. The control plane enforces model allow-lists, so you won't accidentally route to unknown versions.
[14:00] Tom: Let's talk about regional outages. Say: us-east goes down, how do client SDKs reconnect to another region without dropping ongoing conversations?
[14:40] Priya: There are two common patterns: 1) client-side retry with sticky session ID that server uses to load cached KV from a backup store (longer latency), 2) server-side active replication of short-lived KV to warm standby (cheaper for latency, more complex). We recommend approach 2 for low-latency interactive workloads.
[15:20] Maya: Replication sounds expensive. How does that impact cost? We're trying to justify Dedicated vs Hosted.
[16:00] Alex: Replication increases network and storage cost; Dedicated reserves capacity so you pay for the nodes whether used or not. Hosted is cheaper TCO for intermittent loads but Dedicated wins for predictable throughput and tighter SLOs. We'll run cost modeling in the worksheet.
[16:40] Evan: On the compliance side, we need log redaction controls and retention windows. Can Redwood provide per-route retention policies?
[17:20] Priya: Yes, retention is configurable per project/route, and we can redact PII at ingest or at storage. For Private deployments you control retention via your own storage when integrated with our private control plane.
[18:00] Tom: What about circuit breakers and backpressure? If your queue depth crosses threshold, do you fail fast or queue? We prefer graceful failures rather than long tail latencies.
[18:40] Priya: Our runtime supports circuit breakers and smart queuing. Policies can be set to fail fast, enqueue with priority, or degrade immediately to a cheaper model. We can simulate your traffic profile to tune thresholds.
[19:20] Maya: Are there outage modes where some endpoints remain functional and others are blocked? We want partial-service guarantees for critical endpoints.
[20:00] Alex: Yes, route-level SLOs let you prioritize critical endpoints. During resource constraints we steer noncritical routes to low-cost models or rate-limit them while preserving capacity for critical flows.
[20:40] Tom: On the topic of fallbacks, do you have an ability to do model-chain fallbacks? Example: try full 8-bit model, fallback to 4-bit, then finally to a cached response.
[21:20] Priya: Exactly. Fallback chains are configurable — you can set ordered fallbacks with conditions based on latency, error type, or model availability. You can also configure response templates for degraded mode to explain degraded quality to users.
[22:00] Evan: For security we need mTLS mutual auth and SSO into your console. SAML/Okta integration?
[22:40] Alex: We support SAML/Okta and OIDC for the console and RBAC for token scoping. Mutual TLS is supported for dedicated/private network paths.
[23:20] Maya: There was mention of ephemeral tokens per request in the docs—does that exist? We want short-lived auth tokens for front-end to call edge.
[24:00] Priya: Yes, you can issue ephemeral tokens with a limited TTL and scope. These are generated by the control plane and can be rotated automatically.
[24:40] Tom: Okay good. For a pilot, we want to run a regional failover test and a degradation test where we intentionally drop capacity. What's a realistic pilot timeline?
[25:20] Alex: Typical pilot is 4 weeks: week 1 onboarding + config, week 2 bench testing, week 3 pilot with traffic and failover drills, week 4 iterate & finalize SLA mapping.
[26:00] Evan: Any special audit support during pilot? We need log exports to S3 and evidence for our compliance team.
[26:40] Priya: We can provide log exports, request traces, and an audit package. For Private we can store logs in your VPC bucket.
[27:20] Maya: On observability — can we get token-level cost breakdowns and per-request latency heatmaps?
[28:00] Alex: Yep, Redwood Console provides token-level cost, per-route latency histograms, model fallback rate, and we can stream traces to your tracing system.
[28:40] Tom: We have a question about cold starts when scaling up a model — what's the penalty and are there warm-pools?
[29:20] Priya: Cold starts vary — a large context window model will take longer to warm. We support warm-pools and pre-warmed containers for Dedicated to reduce cold start. Also continuous batching helps amortize token cost.
[30:00] Maya: Is there a way to throttle lower-priority traffic automatically during incidents?
[30:40] Priya: Yes, rate-limit policies at route level and dynamic throttling based on circuit-breaker signals are supported.
[31:20] Tom: Let's discuss cost tradeoffs — if we want 99.95% across two regions with replication, that seems pricey. Can you propose mixed strategy?
[32:00] Alex: Mixed strategy: active-active across two regions for critical endpoints, active-passive for less critical, and degraded-model fallback to keep latency while lowering cost. We'll show cost bands in the worksheet.
[32:40] Evan: For the dedicated nodes, what's the SLA for GPU failures and node replacements? We need guaranteed replacement times in the contract.
[33:20] Priya: For Dedicated we offer SLA-backed uptime and defined MTTR windows; hardware replacement SLAs vary by commit tier. We'll include that in the Dedicated term sheet.
[34:00] Maya: On long-running conversations with big KV caches, do you recommend session sharding or single session affinity?
[34:40] Priya: Sharding is more resilient; single affinity gives best per-request latency. If you shard, make sure the client tracks shard keys. We'll help you design the session model.
[35:20] Tom: We also want to capture the runbook steps for common incidents — e.g., region slow, queue spike, or model degraded. Do you provide runbook templates?
[36:00] Alex: Yes, we have operational playbooks and incident templates. We can tailor them to your topology and share an incident cadence example.
[36:40] Evan: A little nit — our compliance team wants stronger encryption in transit. Can you confirm TLS versions and cipher suites?
[37:20] Priya: We support modern TLS 1.2+ with configurable cipher suites for Private and Dedicated. We'll share the exact cipher list in the security pack.
[38:00] Maya: For the benchmarking you'll run, can you replicate our token distribution? Our traffic has many short 8–20 token requests and a long tail of 1k+ tokens.
[38:40] Priya: We'll import your sample traces or you can provide a synthetic profile. Priya: (laugh) I'll add that to the benchmark setup — include head and tail token distribution.
[39:20] Tom: If we fail over to a quantized variant, do you have regression metrics precomputed or do we have to run evals?
[40:00] Priya: We run evals automatically against your prompt set and report several metrics — BLEU-ish quality proxies, repetition/hallucination flags, and customer-defined pass/fail checks. We can also stage canaries to compare live metrics.
[40:40] Evan: Any blockers for us to start a pilot next week? Licensing? Network peering?
[41:20] Alex: No blockers technically. We'll need an NDA and a small pilot contract for Dedicated capacity or a hosted trial for hosted API. Network peering is optional but recommended for lower latency.
[42:00] Maya: For Private deployment, how long is the install and what resources do we need on prem?
[42:40] Priya: On-prem installs vary; typical lead is 6–10 weeks including network setup, hardware procurement, and validation. We'll provide a checklist for infra and NIC requirements.
[43:20] Tom: Last bit — can we get a sample SLA mapping that shows exact behavior at 99.99, 99.95, 99.9 and what fallbacks trigger at each band?
[44:00] Alex: We'll produce an SLA mapping matrix — which routes get active-active, which degrade to smaller models, and how error budgets are consumed. We'll send that as part of the follow-up.
[44:40] Evan: Great. I also want the compliance pack and the list of endpoints for the control plane.
[45:20] Alex: Noted. We'll attach the security pack and a list of public endpoints plus peering IPs.
[46:00] Priya: For the benchmark we'll run with the same token distribution and do an induced regional failover test to measure end-to-end p95 and fallback latency.
[46:40] Tom: Sounds good. Any final questions?
[47:20] Maya: Just a quick one — do you have references for other customers who ran similar region failover pilots?
[48:00] Alex: Yes, we'll share anonymized references and a short case study. Thanks all — we'll follow up with the worksheet and security pack.

Meeting end.
